mappings.note: Discussing Tagore's and Aurobindo's lines on many becoming one is the chapter's central claim about India's human diversity and the attitude to take to it, which is LO-166.
Panchatantra stories and their continuing message, plus similar tales from the pupil's own region: content of an ancient literary work (LO-161) set beside local variety (LO-166).
Collecting folk tales from one's own region is first a description of local diversity (LO-166); the tales themselves are the literary material (LO-161).
An ancient story met through sculpture, dance or film - the epic's content (LO-161) surviving in many regional art forms (LO-166).
Nehru's observation that villagers everywhere knew the epics by heart: the works themselves (LO-161) as the common thread through a diverse country (LO-166).
What strikes visitors first about India - its cultural diversity. The plainest statement of LO-166 in the chapter.
About 325 languages counted by the People of India project; a measured form of India's human diversity, so LO-166.
Vincent Smith finding an underlying unity beneath the diversity - the 'healthy attitude' half of LO-166, seen from an outsider's viewpoint.
Defines 'unity in diversity' as oneness amid variety rather than the erasure of difference; the concept LO-166 is built on.
Rules out quinoa from India's shared staples - the item tests what is COMMON across the country's varied cuisines, so LO-166.
Turmeric, cumin and ginger as the spices used everywhere; again the unity running through diverse regional food.
How the same ingredients yield countless regional dishes - the explicit unity-in-diversity reading of Indian food, hence LO-166.

The sari as one unstitched length of cloth; the shared base from which the chapter's diversity of drapes is drawn. Not LO-174, which is reserved here for Indian textiles as a contribution recognised abroad.
Rejects Egyptian cotton among Banarasi, Kanjivaram and Patan Patola - the item is a roll-call of India's regional silk traditions, so LO-166.
Hundreds of sari varieties as diversity WITHIN one tradition - the chapter's thesis in miniature, squarely LO-166.
Dates the sari from a stone relief at Vaishali: an archaeological source used to fix a date (LO-159) for a living garment tradition (LO-166). The other sari items need no evidence-handling.
Indian chintz so sought after in 17th-century Europe that it was banned - India's contribution in craft carried abroad, which LO-174 covers. Not LO-166: the point is the export, not internal variety.
New draping styles showing the sari is still evolving; diversity as something living rather than fixed, so LO-166.
The sari's many uses beyond dress, showing versatility and everyday ingenuity - part of the same description of a shared but varied tradition.
Makara Sankranti as a harvest festival kept under many names - the festival strand of the chapter's diversity argument.
Pongal placed in Tamil Nadu; a regional name for the same festival, so LO-166. Not LO-156, whose States are to be identified on a map, not paired with a festival.
Magh Bihu placed in Assam - the north-eastern name for the same harvest festival, mapped with Pongal under LO-166.
The Panchatantra in 200 adaptations across 50 languages: an ancient Indian work (LO-161) whose travel abroad is India's contact with other regions (LO-173).
Names the Ramayana and Mahabharata as the two Sanskrit epics - a fact about the literary works of the time, so LO-161.
The Pandavas against their Kaurava cousins; an event inside a named epic, which LO-161 covers explicitly.
Ravana's abduction of Sita - again an event and a personality within an epic, hence LO-161.
Folk and tribal retellings showing how deep the epics reach: the works (LO-161) recast by many communities (LO-166).
Names the Bhils, Gonds and Mundas as communities with their own epic versions - the item is first about which communities (LO-166) and then about the epics (LO-161).
The epics spreading across Asia in many adaptations: contact with regions outside India (LO-173) offered as the clearest case of one becoming many (LO-166).
Defines pigments as the colouring substances in textiles - vocabulary belonging to the sari and chintz material, so it sits with the diversity items.
Article 1's 'India, that is Bharat'. This is a Constitution item; none of CG-SST3's outcomes reaches the naming of the Union, so the goal is the honest altitude.
Matches each harvest festival to its region and finds Magh Bihu with Assam; regional variety of a shared festival, so LO-166.
Assertion-reason that diversity enriches rather than divides, through 'Many in the One' - the attitude clause of LO-166 stated outright.
Finds the false claim that the sari is worn in one style; the item turns on recognising variety in food, dress, festivals and epics alike.
Statement set on the dhoti as unstitched and sari fabrics (LO-166) together with chintz as a major export (LO-174), which is why both are cited.
Defines an epic as a long heroic narrative poem - the literary category the Ramayana and Mahabharata belong to, so LO-161.
Tribal legends tying local history to the Pandavas read as a sense of shared heritage: diverse communities (LO-166) claiming a place in the epic tradition (LO-161).
Twenty-five scripts implying a long written tradition; the script count is another measure of India's diversity, so LO-166.
'Many in the One' as fundamental unity amid variety - the chapter's title phrase, and the core of LO-166.
Identifies the Patan Patola double-ikat sari from its place of making; a regional craft tradition, so LO-166 with the other sari items.
